# Editorial overview

## Read before code: problem dossiers

**A. Capstone Subset.** Split items in half. Every full subset is one pair of
half-subsets; sorted right sums let each left sum find its best legal partner.
Test empty subset, exact limit, and all items above the limit.

**B. Capstone CRT.** Maintain one residue/modulus pair for processed equations.
Compatibility is residue agreement modulo the gcd; extended Euclid constructs
the merged pair. Test compatible non-coprime moduli and an impossible pair.

**C. Capstone Recurrence.** The adjacent Fibonacci pair is the invariant;
doubling identities process index bits. Test zero and values around a power of
two. Each query is `O(log n)`.

## Problem-specific proof map

**A. Capstone Subset.** Every subset splits uniquely into a left-half and a
right-half subset. Sorting right sums and taking the greatest compatible one
for every left sum examines the optimum in `O(2^{n/2} log 2^{n/2})` time.

**B. Capstone CRT.** The current pair `(a,m)` represents exactly all solutions
to processed congruences. A new congruence is compatible iff residues agree
modulo `gcd(m,n)`; extended Euclid then constructs its merged residue.

**C. Capstone Recurrence.** The fast-doubling invariant stores adjacent
Fibonacci values. The identities preserve it when a binary digit doubles or
doubles-plus-one the index, yielding logarithmic queries.

## Detailed solution guide

**A. Capstone Subset Optimization.** Split the items into two halves, enumerate
all subset sums of each half, and sort the right-half sums. For every left sum,
binary-search the best right partner that keeps the total under the limit. This
is the meet-in-the-middle proof from Section 47: every full subset has exactly
one left subset and one right subset.

**B. Capstone Congruences.** Merge congruences one at a time with CRT. At each
step, the current pair `(a,m)` represents all numbers satisfying the processed
constraints. Merging with `(b,n)` either detects incompatible residues modulo
`gcd(m,n)` or produces a new residue modulo `lcm(m,n)` representing the
intersection. This invariant makes the final answer immediate.

**C. Capstone Recurrence.** Use fast doubling to evaluate the recurrence in
logarithmic time. The state pair stores adjacent Fibonacci values, the doubling
formula advances from `k` to `2k`, and the optional step advances to `2k+1`.
Processing all bits of `n` therefore computes the requested value exactly.

**Common pitfalls.** The final capstone intentionally mixes techniques. Write
the invariant for each module separately, test it locally, then combine the
outputs only after each module is correct on its own.

The capstone revisits three patterns that should now be automatic.

- A uses meet-in-the-middle for maximum subset sum under a limit.
- B merges congruences by generalized CRT and rejects incompatible residues.
- C answers recurrence queries with fast Fibonacci doubling.

The final proof style is concise but complete: define the compressed object,
prove it preserves the original choices, and show every query reads the desired
value from that object.

# A. Capstone Subset

## Restatement

Meet-in-the-middle: maximum subset sum not exceeding `X`.

## Observations and algorithm

Split the array into two halves and enumerate all subset sums of each. Sort the
right sums; for each left sum binary-search the greatest right partner not
exceeding `X-left`. Trace an empty right subset and an exact-limit pair.

## Correctness proof

Every full subset decomposes uniquely into one subset of each half. The binary
search considers the best feasible partner for each left choice, including the
optimal decomposition. $\square$

## Complexity

Time `O(2^(n/2) log 2^(n/2))`, memory `O(2^(n/2))`. Use `long long` sums; test
the empty subset and values larger than the limit.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; vector<long long>sums(vector<long long>a){vector<long long>r{0};for(long long x:a){int m=r.size();for(int i=0;i<m;i++)r.push_back(r[i]+x);}return r;}int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);int n;long long x;if(!(cin>>n>>x))return 0;vector<long long>a(n);for(auto&v:a)cin>>v;vector<long long>l(a.begin(),a.begin()+n/2),rr(a.begin()+n/2,a.end());auto L=sums(l),R=sums(rr);sort(R.begin(),R.end());long long best=0;for(long long s:L){auto it=upper_bound(R.begin(),R.end(),x-s);if(it!=R.begin()){--it;best=max(best,s+*it);}}cout<<best<<'\n';}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys,bisect
def sums(a):
    res=[0]
    for x in a: res += [y+x for y in res]
    return res
def main():
    data=list(map(int,sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data: return
    n,x=data[0],data[1]; a=data[2:]; left=sums(a[:n//2]); right=sorted(sums(a[n//2:])); best=0
    for s in left:
        i=bisect.bisect_right(right,x-s)-1
        if i>=0: best=max(best,s+right[i])
    print(best)
if __name__=="__main__": main()
```

# B. Capstone CRT

## Restatement

Merge pairs of congruences or report impossibility.

## Observations and algorithm

Maintain `x == a (mod m)` for processed equations. To merge `b (mod n)`, first
require `(b-a)` divisible by `gcd(m,n)`, then use extended Euclid to solve the
reduced multiplier and normalize modulo the lcm.

## Correctness proof

The divisibility condition is necessary because both residues must agree modulo
the gcd; the constructed multiplier satisfies both equations, so the merged
class represents exactly their intersection. $\square$

## Complexity

Extended Euclid costs `O(log min(m,n))`. Use wide multiplication for the lcm;
test compatible non-coprime moduli and incompatible residues.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; long long eg(long long a,long long b,long long&x,long long&y){if(!b){x=a>=0?1:-1;y=0;return llabs(a);}long long x1,y1,g=eg(b,a%b,x1,y1);x=y1;y=x1-a/b*y1;return g;}int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);int T;if(!(cin>>T))return 0;while(T--){long long a,m,b,n,x,y;cin>>a>>m>>b>>n;long long g=eg(m,n,x,y);if((b-a)%g)cout<<"NO\n";else{long long l=m/g*n;__int128 k=(__int128)((b-a)/g)*x;long long mod=n/g;long long kk=(long long)((k%mod+mod)%mod);long long res=(long long)(((__int128)a+(__int128)m*kk)%l);cout<<res<<" "<<l<<"\n";}}}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys,math
def eg(a,b):
    if b==0: return (abs(a),1 if a>=0 else -1,0)
    g,x,y=eg(b,a%b); return g,y,x-(a//b)*y
def main():
    data=list(map(int,sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data: return
    t=data[0]; idx=1; out=[]
    for _ in range(t):
        a,m,b,n=data[idx],data[idx+1],data[idx+2],data[idx+3]; idx+=4; g,x,y=eg(m,n)
        if (b-a)%g: out.append("NO")
        else:
            l=m//g*n; k=((b-a)//g*x)%(n//g); out.append(f"{(a+m*k)%l} {l}")
    print("\n".join(out))
if __name__=="__main__": main()
```

# C. Capstone Recurrence

## Restatement

Fast Fibonacci queries modulo `1e9+7`.

## Observations and algorithm

Use fast doubling with state `(F(k),F(k+1))`. From it compute values at `2k`,
then choose the even or odd pair according to the current index bit.

## Correctness proof

The doubling identities are algebraic Fibonacci identities; induction on the
halved index proves the state remains adjacent Fibonacci values. $\square$

## Complexity

`O(log n)` time and recursion depth per query. Test `0`, `1`, and a large
power-of-two boundary.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; const long long MOD=1000000007; pair<long long,long long> fib(long long n){if(!n)return{0,1};auto [a,b]=fib(n/2);long long c=a*((2*b%MOD-a+MOD)%MOD)%MOD,d=(a*a%MOD+b*b%MOD)%MOD;return n&1?make_pair(d,(c+d)%MOD):make_pair(c,d);}int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);int t;if(!(cin>>t))return 0;while(t--){long long n;cin>>n;cout<<fib(n).first<<'\n';}}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys
MOD=1_000_000_007
def fib(n):
    if n==0: return (0,1)
    a,b=fib(n//2)
    c=a*((2*b-a)%MOD)%MOD
    d=(a*a+b*b)%MOD
    return (d,(c+d)%MOD) if n%2 else (c,d)
def main():
    data=list(map(int,sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data: return
    print("\n".join(str(fib(x)[0]) for x in data[1:1+data[0]]))
if __name__=="__main__": main()
```

# D. Coupon Route

## State expansion

The free-edge coupon is part of the route history. Reaching the same vertex
before and after using it are different situations, so use states `(vertex,used)`
where `used` is zero or one. From `(v,used)`, an edge of weight `w` gives
`(to,used)` at cost `w`; when `used=0`, it also gives `(to,1)` at cost zero.

All expanded-edge costs are nonnegative, so run Dijkstra from `(1,0)`. The
answer is the smaller distance to `(n,0)` and `(n,1)`.

## Correctness proof

Every legal original route maps to exactly one expanded path by marking whether
its coupon has already been used. Its expanded cost equals its paid cost.
Conversely, every expanded path uses at most one zero-cost coupon transition,
so it maps to a legal route of the same cost. Dijkstra returns shortest paths
in this nonnegative expanded graph; therefore the reported minimum is optimal.

## Complexity and tests

The expanded graph has `2n` states and at most `4m` directed transitions, so
Dijkstra costs `O((n+m) log n)` time and `O(n+m)` memory. Test one edge (answer
zero), a route where the most expensive edge is not on the ordinary shortest
path, and a long chain. The tiny oracle uses repeated edge relaxation on both
coupon layers; the scale case is a 200000-vertex chain.
